title: Coarctation of the aorta and interrupted aortic arch: anatomy, repair and recoarctation
subject: ss-ctvs
refs: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 22e Ch 117 (Congenital Heart Disease: Aortic Arch Anomalies)
Kirklin/Barratt-Boyes Cardiac Surgery 4e Ch 40 (Coarctation of the Aorta and Interrupted Aortic Arch)
AHA/ACC Guidelines for the Management of Adults With Congenital Heart Disease

steps.say: Coarctation of the aorta is a localized narrowing of the aortic lumen. The lesion is typically located in the aortic isthmus, immediately adjacent to the ductus arteriosus or ligamentum arteriosum. Ectopic ductal tissue encircling the aorta contracts after birth, causing severe narrowing.
steps.tx: Aortic coarctation presents as a discrete narrowing of the aortic lumen, characteristically positioned at the **aortic isthmus** adjacent to the ductus arteriosus. The underlying embryology involves migration of **ductal tissue constriction** into the aortic media, closing the lumen as the ductus contracts.

left.title: Juxtaductal Coarctation
points: Discrete shelflike posterior infolding at the isthmus
Adjacent to ductus arteriosus / ligamentum arteriosum
Overwhelmingly common anatomical presentation in older children and adults

right.title: Tubular Hypoplasia of the Arch
points: Long-segment diffuse narrowing of distal transverse arch
Frequently associated with ventricular septal defect
Prevalent in neonates presenting with cardiogenic collapse

steps.tx: The inset in this illustration explains a plain radiograph sign students often memorise without seeing its mechanism. Long standing **rib notching** develops where dilated intercostal collateral arteries erode the inferior margins of the posterior ribs as blood bypasses the narrowed isthmus. Beside it, the main view shows the discrete juxtaductal shelf with dilatation just beyond the stenosis, linking anatomy, collateral flow and the femoral delay felt clinically.
steps.say: Rib notching comes from dilated intercostal collaterals bypassing a juxtaductal coarctation. The main view pairs the stenotic shelf with post stenotic dilatation.

vis.alt: Aortic coarctation at the isthmus with post stenotic dilatation and an inset of rib notching from collateral arteries
vis.caption: Juxtaductal coarctation with post stenotic dilatation fills the main view, while an inset shows rib notching from collaterals. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.say: Physical examination reveals and confirms classic hemodynamic hallmarks. Patients demonstrate significant upper extremity hypertension accompanied by diminished or absent femoral pulses. A radiofemoral pulse delay and a blood pressure gradient exceeding twenty millimeters of mercury confirm the diagnosis.
steps.tx: Clinical diagnosis rests on finding **upper extremity hypertension** paired with diminished, delayed femoral pulses. The presence of a notable **radiofemoral delay** and a systolic **blood pressure gradient** exceeding 20 mmHg between the right arm and lower extremities establishes hemodynamically significant coarctation.

rows: Indicates severe flow restriction across the isthmus
Reflects delayed wave reflection through collateral networks
Turbulent high-velocity flow over isthmus and chest collateral beds

steps.say: Aortic coarctation frequently occurs with other cardiovascular malformations. Up to eighty percent of patients have a congenital bicuspid aortic valve. In addition, patients frequently develop intracranial saccular aneurysms in the circle of Willis, carrying a life-threatening risk of subarachnoid hemorrhage.
steps.tx: Coarctation exhibits powerful anatomical associations: over 50 to 80 percent of patients harbor a **bicuspid aortic valve**. Furthermore, patients exhibit an elevated risk of **berry aneurysms** in the circle of Willis, predisposing to catastrophic **intracranial hemorrhage** even after successful coarctation repair.

rows: Accelerated aortic stenosis, regurgitation, and root aortopathy
Life-threatening subarachnoid hemorrhage; warrants MRA screening
Massive left-to-right shunt and early congestive heart failure

steps.say: Chronic aortic obstruction prompts extensive collateral vascular remodeling. Intercostal arteries, internal thoracic arteries, and scapular vessels dilate to carry blood around the obstruction. Pulsatile enlarged intercostal arteries erode the inferior rib margins, producing classic rib notching on chest radiographs.
steps.tx: Longstanding severe coarctation promotes extensive compensatory collateral vessels through internal mammary and intercostal arteries. Enlarged, tortuous intercostal vessels erode the inferior cortex of the third to eighth ribs, producing characteristic **rib notching** (Roesler sign) and the aortic **figure-of-3 sign**. Recognizing these pathognomonic collateral signs on routine imaging alerts clinicians to severe hemodynamically significant aortic narrowing.

nodes.label: Severe mechanical obstruction at aortic isthmus
Flow diversion into internal mammary and subclavian arteries
Massive tortuous dilatation of posterior intercostal vessels
Inferior rib cortical bone erosion producing visible rib notching

steps.say: In critical neonatal coarctation, systemic lower body perfusion depends on ductal patency. When the ductus arteriosus constricts, neonates present with severe metabolic acidosis, anuria, and cardiogenic shock. An immediate continuous prostaglandin E1 infusion reopens the ductus, restoring lower body perfusion.
steps.tx: In ductal-dependent neonatal coarctation, ductal closure precipitates sudden cardiogenic shock, profound oliguria, and worsening metabolic acidosis. Emergency medical stabilization requires immediate intravenous **prostaglandin E1** (alprostadil) infusion. Prostaglandin rapidly reopens the constricted **ductus arteriosus**, restoring systemic **lower body perfusion** before definitive surgical repair.

nodes.label: Neonatal presentation with shock, absent pulses, and acidosis
Start prostaglandin E1 infusion (0.01 to 0.05 mcg/kg/min)
Reopen ductus arteriosus to establish right-to-left lower perfusion
Correct acidosis and transfer to OR for surgical reconstruction

steps.say: Surgical repair aims to establish an unobstructed aortic lumen with native tissue. Resection with extended end-to-end anastomosis is the preferred operation for neonates and infants. The surgeon completely excises all ductal tissue and creates a wide spatulated connection onto the underside of the arch.
steps.tx: The gold standard surgical repair is **extended end-to-end anastomosis**. The surgeon excises the coarctation shelf and all ductal tissue, spatulating the distal descending aorta onto the undersurface of the transverse arch to achieve **complete ductal excision** and eliminate **recoarctation risk**.

left.title: Extended End-to-End Anastomosis
points: Completely resects all ectopic ductal tissue
Enlarges undersurface of transverse aortic arch
Lowest lifetime incidence of late aortic aneurysm formation

right.title: Subclavian Flap Angioplasty (Waldhausen)
points: Divides and turns down left subclavian artery as patch
Sacrifices left subclavian artery flow to left upper limb
Potential for reduced left arm growth and claudication

steps.tx: Coarctation narrows the aorta. Interruption leaves a gap, and the lower body depends on the duct. In an **interrupted aortic arch**, type A is the gap beyond the left subclavian, type B lies between the left carotid and the left subclavian, and type C lies between the carotid arteries. Type B is the common form and travels with DiGeorge syndrome. The neonate collapses as the duct closes. Repair must join the arch. Resecting a shelf is the operation for coarctation, not for a missing segment.
steps.say: Interrupted arch type A lies beyond the left subclavian, type B between the left carotid and the subclavian, and type C between the carotids. Type B is commonest. The duct supplies the lower body until it closes.

vis.alt: Interrupted aortic arch types A, B and C, with the site of the gap marked on each.
vis.caption: Types A, B and C of interrupted aortic arch are shown, with the gap beyond the left subclavian, between the left carotid and the subclavian, or between the carotid arteries. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.say: Interrupted aortic arch is an extreme congenital catastrophe characterized by complete luminal discontinuity. The Celoria and Patton classification classifies it into three types based on the interruption site. Type B, where the gap lies between the left carotid and subclavian arteries, is most common and strongly linked with DiGeorge syndrome.
steps.tx: Interrupted aortic arch exhibits complete anatomical discontinuity between arch segments. The **Celoria-Patton classification** identifies three subtypes: **Type B interruption**, occurring between the left common carotid and subclavian arteries, is most common and strongly associated with **DiGeorge syndrome** and 22q11.2 deletion.

rows: Distal to left subclavian artery (at isthmus)
30 to 40 percent of cases; similar to severe coarctation
Between left common carotid and left subclavian
50 to 60 percent of cases; 22q11.2 DiGeorge deletion association
Between innominate and left common carotid
Rare (< 5 percent); interruption of proximal transverse arch

steps.say: Following surgical repair, patients can develop paradoxical postoperative hypertension and mesenteric arteritis. This condition, termed postcoarctectomy syndrome, stems from acute baroreceptor resetting and sympathetic hyperactivation. Aggressive treatment with intravenous nitroprusside or beta-blockers prevents bowel necrosis.
steps.tx: Postoperatively, acute baroreceptor resetting and sympathetic surges trigger severe **paradoxical hypertension** and necrotizing **mesenteric arteritis**, known as **postcoarctectomy syndrome**. Clinicians manage this hypertensive emergency aggressively using intravenous sodium nitroprusside or beta-blockers to prevent intestinal infarction, bowel necrosis, and prolonged paralytic ileus.

left.title: Postcoarctectomy Pathophysiology
points: Sudden exposure of mesenteric bed to high pulsatile pressure
Reflex sympathetic hyperactivation and baroreceptor resetting
Severe abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, and leukocytosis

right.title: Therapeutic Management Bundle
points: Immediate continuous intravenous sodium nitroprusside infusion
Aggressive oral or IV beta-blocker sympathetic suppression
Nasogastric decompression and bowel rest until symptoms resolve

steps.tx: Once the isthmus is opened, baroreceptors reset abruptly and sympathetic drive surges. The result is severe **paradoxical hypertension** together with necrotizing mesenteric arteritis, the pair called postcoarctectomy syndrome. Intravenous sodium nitroprusside or a beta blocker is used aggressively. The point of that emergency treatment is to prevent intestinal infarction, bowel necrosis and a long paralytic ileus. Inflamed mesenteric branches after a good anatomical repair are this arteritis, not a missed narrowing lower down.
steps.say: After coarctation repair, abrupt baroreceptor resetting and a sympathetic surge cause paradoxical hypertension and necrotizing mesenteric arteritis, called postcoarctectomy syndrome. Nitroprusside or a beta blocker is given intravenously so the bowel does not infarct, necrose or stop moving for a prolonged ileus.

vis.alt: The repaired aortic isthmus is shown with carotid sinus and arch baroreceptors highlighted, while the downstream mesenteric arteries are thickened and inflamed.
vis.caption: After coarctation repair the arch baroreceptors are marked, and the mesenteric arteries beyond the repair are thickened and inflamed. Illustration: StewardMD original.
